To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the loading rate of an indicator into intact fibers depends strongly on the molecular weight, that the time course of Ca2+ transients is similar with AM-loading or microinjection, and that the amplitude of the Ca2+ transient is smaller with AM-loading than with microinjection.

1) the AM-loading rate is strongly dependent on the MW of the AM compound, 2) the loading rate is strongly dependent upon the MW of the free indicator, 3) the AM-loading rates of the indicators studied are too slow to allow accurate measurements of the Ca2+ concentration in the first few minutes after a muscle fiber is exposed to a Ca2+-mobilizing agent, and 4) the loading rate of the indicator must be at least 100 microM/h

the loading rates of AM compounds into frog muscle fibers are strongly dependent on their molecular weight; that the loading rate is the key factor determining the value of f; that the value of f is the key factor in determining the accuracy with which Ca2+ concentration in a muscle fiber can be estimated using AM compounds; and that, with any indicator, the loaded concentration must be large enough to avoid significant error due to nonspecific indicator.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development and application of fluorescent Ca2(+)-sensitive indicators for use in the study of Ca2(+)-dependent processes in living cells.
the loading of fluorescent Ca2+-sensitive indicators in intact muscle cells, and with the properties of Ca2+ transients observed with these indicators.
the development of new fluorescent Ca2+ indicator molecules.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the AM-loading method is a very useful tool for the study of intracellular calcium, provided that loading rates are high enough to avoid the nonspecific association of indicator with the fiber.
the use of AM-loading is a valid and useful technique for the study of Ca2+ in single muscle fibers, provided that the loading rate of the particular indicator is sufficiently large.
the use of AM-loaded cells for Ca2+ measurements should be approached with extreme caution.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

, for the indicators tested, the loading rates were strongly dependent upon molecular weight and, for the larger molecular weight indicators (MW approximately greater than 1,000), loading rates were generally low (<10 microM/hr) and the resulting delta F/F values were small and unreliable.
the AM-loading of a fluorescent Ca2+ indicator is a viable alternative to microinjection, but that the loading rate should be as high as possible, consistent with other requirements.
the use of AM-loading is a useful and convenient method for studying [Ca2+] in intact fibers.
The main takeaway from our work is that
, for a given AM indicator, the rate of loading should be determined before the indicator is used for Ca2+ measurements in single muscle fibers.
, to minimize this source of error, the loading rate should be as large as possible, and that this is best achieved by using AM compounds of low molecular weight.
the loading rate is an important indicator of the suitability of a given AM indicator for measuring [Ca2+] in intact muscle fibers.
